title: Vertical scaling
idea: Vertical scaling means giving one machine more CPU, memory or disk, so the same app handles more load without any change to its code.

analogy.text: Replacing a delivery van with a bigger truck. One driver, one vehicle, more cargo per trip. Nothing about the route or the driver changes.
analogy.breaks: Trucks stop getting bigger; servers have a largest size too.

points: You resize the machine or move to a bigger instance type.
The app and its data stay on one machine, so nothing needs redesign.
Every machine has a ceiling, and the biggest sizes cost disproportionately more.
Resizing often means a restart, and one machine is still one point of failure.

hero.title: Why it is easy, and where it stops

left.title: What you gain
items: No code changes: the app runs as before
No new moving parts to operate
Local memory and files still work
Often a fast first fix for slow responses

right.title: What you hit
items: A hardware ceiling: the largest machine available
Cost grows faster than capacity at the top
Resizing may restart the machine and cause downtime
If the machine fails, the whole app is down

hero.verdict: Vertical scaling is the simplest step, not a path without an end.

pitfalls: Do not assume a bigger machine fixes slow queries; check the real bottleneck first.
Plan a maintenance window before resizing; the machine may restart.
Do not treat one large server as high availability; it can still fail.

quiz.q: You move a slow app to one machine with twice the CPU and memory. What is still true?
options: Traffic is now spread across two servers
A single failure still takes the whole app down
You can keep doing this with no upper limit
The app must be rewritten to be stateless
quiz.why: Vertical scaling makes one machine bigger. It stays a single point of failure, has a ceiling, and needs no code changes.

takeaway: Vertical scaling is simple, but it has a ceiling and one point of failure.
